Campbell’s Soup Cans

Andy Warhol’s thirty-two canvases, each a single Campbell’s soup can in the same format, one for each variety the company then sold.

Source
MoMA: Andy Warhol, Campbell’s Soup Cans, 1962
Creator
Andy Warhol
Made
1962
Style
Pop art (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Commercial, deadpan, repetitive
Evidence
MoMA’s collection page blocks scripts, and no open image of at least 800 px was found. Description relies on Wikipedia and on the MoMA record as quoted in search results.
Reviewed
28 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The series has 32 paintings, each showing a different variety of Campbell’s soup in a uniform 20 × 16 inch format. It was first shown in July 1962 at the Ferus Gallery, Los Angeles, and the Museum of Modern Art acquired the canvases in 1996. Wikipedia.

Wikipedia quotes MoMA that Warhol “was careful to maintain an exceptional uniformity among the canvases and to minimize the visibility of brushstrokes or other signs of his own hand.” Wikipedia.

In 1967 Campbell’s promoted its soup with a paper dress printed after the series: “Souper” paper dress.

Why it belongs

The series defines the product branch of Pop art: an everyday package isolated, enlarged, and repeated, with the hand of the painter hidden.

For a screen layout, it suggests identical cards in a strict grid in which only the label text changes.

Borrow

Build a catalogue grid of identical product cards and change only the name on each card.

Keep the product front-on and centered in every cell, with no perspective or shadow.
